newsitem.title: UK: POLL - UK unemployment to tumble in June.
newsitem.headline: POLL - UK unemployment to tumble in June.

text.p: Strong economic growth means British unemployment probably tumbled again in June, but average earnings growth held steady, economists said on Monday.
A Reuter poll of economists produced a consensus that the number of jobless fell by 25,000 last month, continuing the trend of substantial falls seen over the last year.

"We expect to see the labour market continue to tighten at a rapid rate in June," said Darshini David, UK economist at HSBC Markets. She forecast a net 30,000 people were taken off the dole queues over the month.

In June last year, Office for National Statistics data put the total number of jobless at 2.17 million. In May, that total had shrunk to 1.64 million after a 18,400 monthly fall. The latest figures will be released at 0830 GMT on Wednesday.

But the pace of falling unemployment may be slowing a little -- May's unemployment fall was the first monthly drop of less than 30,000 since August last year -- but that is probably more to do with systemic distortions rather than a slowdown in actual job creation.

"The shift in trend reflected the waning effect of the new JobSeekers' allowance, which is no longer having such a big effect on the monthly changes in unemployment," said Michael Saunders, UK economist at Salomon Brothers.

The JSA, which replaced old-style unemployment benefit last year, tightened up the requirements for those claiming benefit. The switch to a new system created a huge backlog of claims which remained unprocessed for months and flattered the jobless figures.
As a result, unemployment in June will have dropped more slowly than has been the case in recent months, Saunders said. He forecast a 20,000 drop.
"Nevertheless, such a figure would put the jobless total only a whisker above the low seen at the end of the last cycle and hence keep fears alive that the labour market is tightening."
The jobless rate bottomed at 5.6 percent in 1990. Last month the rate was 5.8 percent. But things may be different now.

A Reuter survey of 26 economists, released on Monday, showed the average of predictions forecast a fall in the jobless rate to 5.1 percent by the end of 1998. Nine of the analysts expected it to drop below five percent.
David expected the number of job vacancies to rise by a further 5,000 in June. That showed the robustness of the labour market, she said.

Annual average earnings growth is forecast to hold steady at 4.5 percent in May although Saunders said there was a chance earnings growth could drop to 4.25 percent as the upwards effects of early-year bonus payments faded out of the equation.

But he said the buoyant economy would tend to push up wage drift -- the difference between pay settlements and overall earnings growth. That will offset some of the downward impact of the bonus effect.
Andrew Cates, UK economist at UBS, expected steady earnings growth. "Pay settlements have recently been steady," he said.

Unit wage costs are expected to hold fairly steady in May, growing by 2.3 percent in the latest three months compared with 2.2 percent in the three months to April. But they should show a hefty monthly rise because manufacturing output dropped sharply, by 1.1 percent, in May.
"This could be the first sign that the appreciation of sterling is finally having an adverse effect on manufacturing output," David said.
